To fix Codebook Check

What we found

  • We parsed 5 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
  • 0 of 637 data columns (0%) are documented in a codebook; 637 are not.
  • A codebook was found and parsed (5 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents haplotype, pop1, pop2 while the data has group, gene, allele. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.
Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 5 codebook/README/label sources and 637 data columns across 90 files.

A codebook was found and parsed (5 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents haplotype, pop1, pop2 while the data has group, gene, allele. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.

Code Comments

Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code).

Missing Files

All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 29 distinct packages/libraries: argparse, bs4, concurrent, csv, data.table, devtools, dplyr, fs, ggplot2, ggstance, glob, glue, gzip, logging, magrittr, numpy, os, pandas, pysam, re, readr, requests, scipy, sys, threading, time, tqdm, typing, urllib. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

Reproducible Environment

No renv.lock file, sessionInfo()/session_info() record, or groundhog/checkpoint date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an renv.lock (via the renv package), a sessionInfo() text dump, or a groundhog/checkpoint date-pin alongside the code.

The repository lists the Python packages the code needs in environment.yml.

Table_S10.txt

Group Code Locus Allele Tier Category Effect Notes
AFR A A*36:01 1 HIV Susceptibility Associated with high viral load in HIV seroconverters in Zambian cohorts
AMRN A A*68:03 1 HIV Susceptibility Identified as HIV risk allele in Mesoamerican populations
AFR A A*74:01 1 HIV Protective Associated with lower viral load, higher CD4+ count, and strong protection from HIV-1 acquisition/progression; consistently protective across multiple African cohorts
EUR B B*14:01 1 HIV Protective B27 supertype member; Bw6 allele associated with delayed HIV disease progression
OCE B B*27:04 1 Autoimmune One of the most common AS-associated B27 subtypes; strongly linked to ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and acute anterior uveitis; demonstrates reduced folding rate contributing to ER stress pathogenesis
ASIA B B*27:06 1 Autoimmune Protective/Neutral B27 subtype NOT associated with ankylosing spondylitis; normal folding rate; clinically important for distinguishing pathogenic from benign B27 results
AMR B B*39:06 1 HIV Susceptibility Identified as HIV risk allele in Latin American Mestizo populations
AFR B B*39:10 1 HIV B7 supertype member; presents shared immunodominant TL9 HIV epitope alongside B81:01 and B42:01
AFR B B*42:01 1 HIV Protective Presents multiple Gag epitopes; 0.52 log10 lower viral-load set point vs B42:02; effect ~75% of B57:03
AFRE B B*57:02 1 HIV Protective Protective B57 subtype; differs from B57:03 by one amino acid; hierarchy of protection: B58:01 < B57:02 < B57:03
AFR B B*57:03 1 HIV Protective Strongest HLA class I allele for HIV elite control; most prevalent B*57 subtype in sub-Saharan Africa (~4-5%); drives multiple p24 Gag-specific CD8+ T-cell responses
AFR B B*58:02 1 HIV Susceptibility Strongly correlated with high viral load in clade C infection; disease-susceptibility allele despite close relation to protective B58:01 (differs by 3 amino acids). NOT associated with allopurinol hypersensitivity (that is B58:01)
AFR B B*81:01 1 HIV Protective Bw6 allele associated with delayed HIV disease progression; restricts immunodominant p24 Gag TL9 response; drives escape mutations that reduce viral fitness
ASIA B B*15:02 2 Pharmacogenomic Strongly associated with carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN (OR=113.4); FDA-mandated screening before carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine in Asian-ancestry patients; CPIC guideline exists
CAS B B*15:08 2 Pharmacogenomic HLA-B75 serotype member; shares carbamazepine binding capability with B*15:02; may confer similar SJS/TEN risk
SEAS B B*15:11 2 Pharmacogenomic HLA-B75 serotype member; significant association with carbamazepine-induced SJS after excluding B*15:02 carriers
ASIA A A*02:07 3 Cancer Strongly associated with NPC susceptibility in Chinese populations (OR=2.3); common among Chinese but absent in Caucasians; risk further increased with B*46:01 co-carriage
AFRW B B*27:03 3 Autoimmune B27 subtype; less well-established AS association than B*27:04/05 but part of B27 family warranting clinical attention
ASIA B B*38:02 3 Cancer HLA-B*38:02 associated with increased NPC risk in Taiwanese populations
ASIA B B*46:01 3 Cancer Most significantly associated HLA allele with nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) in Southern Chinese; risk increased further with co-carriage of A*02:07 (OR=2.8); also predicted to have fewest SARS-CoV-2 binding peptides
AFRS DQA1 DQA1*05:02 3 Autoimmune Part of DQ2 haplotype; when combined with DQB1*02, associated with celiac disease susceptibility
AMR DQA1 DQA1*05:03 3 Autoimmune DQA1*05 group member; DQ2-related; potential celiac disease relevance depending on DQB1 pairing
ASIA DQB1 DQB1*04:01 3 Autoimmune Associated with type 1 diabetes risk in some East Asian populations
EUR DRB1 DRB1*01:03 3 Autoimmune Protective DERAA-encoding allele; protective against rheumatoid arthritis
AMR DRB1 DRB1*04:02 3 Autoimmune Protective DERAA-encoding allele; associated with lower susceptibility to rheumatoid arthritis and less severe disease; also classified as protective epitope (PE) allele
EAS DRB1 DRB1*04:06 3 Neurodegeneration DRB104 subtype; weaker protective effects against Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease compared to 04:04 and *04:07
OCE DRB1 DRB1*04:10 3 Autoimmune DRB104 family member; the broader 04 group is associated with RA susceptibility via the shared epitope
AMR DRB1 DRB1*04:11 3 Autoimmune DRB104 family member; the broader 04 group is associated with RA susceptibility via the shared epitope
AFR DRB1 DRB1*08:04 3 Autoimmune Some associations with autoimmune thyroid disease in African populations
AFR DRB1 DRB1*13:04 3 Autoimmune Protective DERAA-encoding allele; protective against rheumatoid arthritis
AFRW DRB1 DRB1*13:04 3 Autoimmune Protective DERAA-encoding allele; protective against rheumatoid arthritis
SEAS DRB1 DRB1*13:12 3 Autoimmune DRB113 group; 13:01 and 13:02 are DERAA alleles protective against RA; 13:12 likely shares some protective properties
AMR DRB1 DRB1*14:02 3 Autoimmune Associated with RA susceptibility in some Native American populations (Pima, Yakima Indians)
CAS DRB1 DRB1*14:03 3 Autoimmune Protective Associated with protective effects against systemic lupus erythematosus in Japanese populations
ASIA DRB1 DRB1*14:04 3 Autoimmune DRB114 group associated with pemphigus vulgaris susceptibility across ethnic groups; DRB114 also protective against multiple sclerosis
AMRN DRB1 DRB1*14:06 3 Autoimmune Associated with leprosy susceptibility in Argentine populations; DRB1*14:06 also identified as protective against systemic sclerosis in Japanese

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 637 columns across 90 data files.

Issues Identified

69 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 90 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

All participants completed informed consent forms approved by relevant ethics review boards and governing agencies in each country of origin.

Ethics approval statement:

All participants completed informed consent forms approved by relevant ethics review boards and governing agencies in each country of origin.

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.
