Methods

Cohort Description and Sample Preparation:

This study aggregated whole-genome sequencing datasets from publicly available sets including the 1kGP 1 , Angola-Mozambique (University of Leicester) 2 The study also included in-house data generated from 8,463 participants that had not previously been analyzed in this way (South Africa -SABR 14 [EGAD50000001477], Madagascar 15 [EGAD50000000708], South Africa -ARK 16 , Aotearoa New Zealand 17 , French Polynesia 18 , Uganda, Indonesia, New Caledonia, and Chile). Participants in these studies were required to be at least 18 years old and willing and able to consent. All participants completed informed consent forms approved by relevant ethics review boards and governing agencies in each country of origin. Where necessary, approvals were obtained for use of controlled-access data (e.g., H3Africa). A full list of cohorts, number of individuals, and source of genomic DNA is provided in Supplemental Table S12. In most cases, genomic DNA originated from whole blood, in some cases from saliva, or, e.g. in the case of 1kGP, from lymphoblastoid cell lines. All sequencing was performed on Illumina platforms with read lengths between 100-150 bp.

Processing of Sequencing Data and Basic QC: Data was processed with an in-house pipeline using GATK Best Practices. We excluded individuals with excessively low effective coverage (<3×) or evidence of contamination (VerifyBamID2 freemix >0.05). Effective coverage is calculated as [Coverage * (1 -Duplicate Rate) * (1 -Contamination)].

Allele Frequency Net Database (AFND) frequencies:

Allele frequencies and content reported in this paper were aggregated using code from the following github repository: https://github.com/slowkow/allelefrequencies.git using a version of the website which was available on July 6th, 2026. Frequencies reported are derived from the gold standard datasets deposited to the AFND, but a table correlating the gold-standard to all derived allele frequencies is available as Supplemental Table S13.

Inclusion of 1kGP children:

Frequencies reported in the manuscript reflect allele frequencies for groups with the 608 children of trios included in the frequencies. While this relatedness skews the sampling design and population representation, we note minimal quantitative changes between the allele frequencies discussed in detail throughout the manuscript both with and without the inclusion of trios. A table with group counts after removal of the children of trios can be found at Supplemental Table S14. A table with allele frequencies both with and without these 608 children can be found in Supplemental Table S30, S31, and S32.

Benchmarking Design:

Algorithms were evaluated on their ability to accurately genotype across all loci in a gene family, performance at various sequencing coverage depths, computational cost, Mendelian consistency, and agreement with orthogonal datasets.

Benchmarking genotyping accuracy across such diverse and divergent regions and against sequence-resolved whole genome assemblies necessitated development of a broadly applicable method for comparison, hap-eval (see below).

HLA Benchmarking (Gold Standard):

HLA typing accuracy on HLA-A, B, and C was evaluated using a recent study of HLA genotypes using targeted exome sequencing 19 . A previous study which leveraged Sanger-derived genotypes 20 was also referenced, but due to its incomplete and noisy nature, was difficult to integrate. Results for the comparison to the 2014 study are in Table S15. We compared three HLA genotyping tools (HLA*LA 21 , Kourami 22 , and exhibited the highest F1-score across all regions at 0.805 which is largely driven by a Recall of 0.968. Full results for this analysis can be found in Table S16. Raw calls for all genotyping methods tested are found in Supplemental Tables S17,S18,S19. The HLA database used for T1K can be found on Zenodo: Supplemental Material S1.

Evaluation of accuracy versus haplotype-based assemblies (hap-eval):

Benchmarking for HLA, IGHC, and Fc Gamma Receptor gene families was conducted against haplotype-resolved assemblies produced by the Human Genome Structural Variant Consortium (HGSVC) 24 , Human Pangenome Reference Consortium (HPRC) 25 , and the Platinum Pedigree project 26 . Predicted genotypes in each region were converted back to sequence resolution predictions which were then aligned back to a common reference genome (GRCh38). Comparable genomic regions were then extracted from the alignment of the assemblies to the same reference genome and alignments were compared against each other via CIGAR strings. With this, false positives (variants relative to GRCh38 in the prediction, but not the assembly), false negatives (variants in the assembly, but not in the prediction), true positives (variants in both the assembly and the prediction), and true negatives (non-variant bases aligning to GRCh38 in the assembly and the prediction) could be determined for each aligned base. Full results can be found in Supplemental Table S2.

Determining the effect of sequencing depth of coverage on number of newly observed alleles: Due to the wide range of sequencing depths of coverage included in the entire cohort, we assessed whether low sequencing coverage generates spurious calls that would incorrectly increase the number of newly observed alleles. To test this, we downsampled the 2,662 individuals from LASI-DAD (part of the South Asian group) to an average depth of coverage of 5× and incorporated those into the results for the rest of the cohort as if these downsampled results were the original calls for this subset.

We selected LASI-DAD for two reasons. First, it is closely size-matched to the Eastern African group (n = 2,593), which contributes the largest number of newly observed alleles (402), so the two are directly comparable without normalization; the downsampled depth of 5× is also comparable to the median depth of the Eastern African group (5.6×). Second, LASI-DAD yields few newly observed alleles at full depth despite its size, so the expected true signal is near zero and alleles appearing only after downsampling can be attributed to depth rather than to genuine group-specific diversity. This makes the comparison maximally sensitive to depth-driven artifacts. We note that this low baseline is consistent with India already being well represented in the AFND, though the argument below depends only on the observed baseline, not on its cause.

Originally, we reported 37 alleles which are group-specific to South Asia and for which no frequency information was available in the AFND across HLA-A, -B, -C, and -DRB1. After downsampling, we report 32 such alleles (Supplemental Figure S2A), of which 22 were shared with the full-depth set. The 15 alleles called only at full depth are largely explained by the downsampled data more frequently reporting a single allele per locus rather than two (Supplemental Figure S2B). Ten newly observed alleles were called only in the downsampled set; these fall within a total of 20 alleles of any kind called only in the downsampled set (Supplemental Figure S2C).

Taking these 10 as an upper bound on depth-driven artifacts in a cohort of ~2,600 samples, low coverage could account for at most ~2.5% of the 402 newly observed alleles in the size-matched Eastern African group. For low coverage to generate the Eastern African signal, the rate of depth-driven artifacts would need to be roughly 40-fold higher there than observed here at matched sample size and comparable depth. We therefore interpret the group differences in newly observed alleles as reflecting representation in the AFND rather than sequencing depth: the AFND contains over 50,000 individuals from India alone, compared with just over 1,000 from the entire continent of Africa.

IGHC Benchmarking (Gold Standard): IGHC benchmarking was conducted for T1K against published sequences for a selection of 1kGP individuals which were sequenced and assembled using long read sequencing (LRS) 27 and hap-eval. Results are summarized in Table S20. (2026-01). As confirmation of this methodology, we looked for presence-absence and geographic distribution of one specific allele: HLA-E*01:152. This allele was first published in May 2025 29 and was observed in low frequency in Southern, Central, and East Africa. GAIA analysis revealed 27 instances of this specific allele (Supplemental Figure S6). All but two of the observations reported in GAIA occurred in Southern, Central, and Western Africa with the other two occurring in South America. Genotyping accuracy for all loci against HGSVC assemblies (hap-eval): 55 samples were selected for their overlap with the HGSVC3 assembly set 24 and availability of raw data.

Genotyping

Genotyping of Fc

Comparisons were made both gene-body wide and in coding regions. Gene body wide statistics are captured in Supplemental Table S24. Coding sequence results are contained in Supplemental Table S25.

Benchmarking universal genotyping tools for IGHC and FCGR: We tested Locityper 30 , T1K 23 , and Ctyper 31 for their general ability to genotype across both IGHC and FCGR genes.

Both Locityper and T1K can receive custom databases or graphs which can be applied genome-wide and Ctyper relies on a pre-computed CNV map incorporating sequence-resolved paralogs. Many, but not all, IGHC and FCGR genes appear in this CNV map. Additionally, vg-giraffe 32 was tested, but runtimes were not feasible for a cohort of this size. While locityper could recover some IGHC genes (IGHG1, IGHGP) with reasonable accuracy (F1-score > 0.75), this analysis revealed that T1K is more capable in these regions while the opposite was true for FCGR. Results for this comparison can be found in Supplemental Table S26.

Benchmarking whole genome vs whole exome sequencing for all loci: In addition to comparisons against gold standard sets, we compared tools for consistency against orthogonal data types. We took 314 internal samples from a Ugandan cohort with whole genome sequencing (WGS) and whole exome sequencing (WES) available and initiated genotyping for T1K and Locityper across all genes of interest. We counted true/false positives/negatives similar to the gold standard analysis with the WGS serving as the gold standard against which to compare WES. For WGS, 32 genomic loci showed F1-scores above 0.75 with 31 coming from the HLA gene family. Analysis with hap-eval revealed a higher level of concordance across all regions due to small mismatches in sequence affecting precision in hap-eval less dramatically as compared to a direct matching of genotype which would result in a precision score of 0 for a sample. Results for the comparison using hap-eval can be found in Supplemental Table S27.

Benchmarking Mendelian consistency: Contained in the 330 1kGP samples were 88 trios.

The children in these trios were compared against genotype calls in the parents to determine

Mendelian consistency across all regions and simulated sequencing depths. Results from this analysis are contained in Supplemental Table S28. Additionally, hap-eval was used to determine actual sequence match between predicted, inherited alleles and parent genotypes. Results for that analysis are found here in Supplemental Table S29.

Majority Allelic Diversity (MAD):

We introduce majority allelic diversity (MAD) as a measure of allelic breadth within a group. MAD-X is the number of alleles required for X% of individuals in a group to carry at least one allele from the set. Carrier status is taken from observed diplotypes rather than inferred from allele frequencies, so no Hardy-Weinberg assumption is made. This matters in admixed and structured groups, where genotype frequencies depart from the expectation under allele frequencies alone. The set is built greedily. Beginning with all genotyped individuals in the group, we select the allele carried by the largest number of them and remove every individual carrying it from the pool. Carrier counts are then recalculated among the individuals who remain, and the allele carried by the largest number of those is added next. Selection therefore depends on the residual pool rather than on frequency in the group as a whole: an allele that is common but largely confined to individuals already covered contributes little and may never be selected. Alleles are added until the cumulative number of individuals covered, as a fraction of the group's original size, reaches or exceeds X%. MAD-X is the size of the resulting set. For example, in a group of 100 individuals, suppose 84 carry allele 001. MAD-50 = 1, since 001 alone exceeds the 50% threshold. Removing those 84 leaves 16 individuals; of these, 12 carry 002, bringing cumulative coverage to 96. MAD-90 = 2.

To extend this to a global measure, we define global MAD-X as the number of unique alleles in the union of all subcontinental MAD-X sets -that is, the total number of alleles needed to simultaneously reach the threshold in every subcontinental group. It should be noted that these numbers can be highly skewed by unequal sampling and population sizes; these figures are meant to be starting points for approaching understanding diversity and vaccine development.

In order to directly understand the distribution of HLA alleles in a given population, more direct sampling would be required.

Measuring per locus diversity with MAD-50:

Global MAD-50 values represent the total number of unique alleles across all subcontinental MAD-50 sets in GAIA. Across the eight classical loci surveyed by the AFND, DPA1 has the lowest global MAD-50 (4 alleles). Other loci show even lower allelic diversity, with 15 loci showing a global MAD-50 of 1 (Supplemental Table S7). All of these exist outside of the scope of alleles reported to the AFND and this diversity is reported in GAIA for the first time. All of these regions are contained in the HLA family of genes and there are only 9 loci in HLA which show a MAD-50 above 4: A, B, C, DPB1, DQA1, DQB1, DRB1, MICA, and H. All IGHC and FCGR loci we examined had a global MAD-50 greater than 4, however, MAD-50 should not be confused with fixation of specific alleles. For example, at IGHG1 all subcontinental groups show a MAD-50 between 1 and 3, but there are still alleles which are more common in specific subcontinental groups over others as highlighted in the main text and with a global MAD-50 of 8 (Supplemental Figure S3). Among all loci surveyed, FCGBP has the highest global MAD-50 value of 137 followed by FCGR3A and FCGR2C at 118 and 116 respectively.

HLA-B has the highest mean MAD-50 among the MHC genes with a value of 3.72 between subcontinental groups, followed by DRB1, A, and C with mean MAD-50 values of 2.94, 2.44, and 2.33, respectively. Across all MHC loci, the Southern African, North American, South American, and Eastern African subcontinental groups show the highest mean MAD-50 of 1.41, 1.41, 1.39 and 1.37 respectively. Across all IGHC loci, the top-four subcontinental group MAD-50 values are the Central African (2.2), Southern African (2.2), North American (2.2), and Western African (2.0) subcontinental groups. For FCGR loci, the top-four subcontinental group MAD-50 values are seen in South America (17.7), North America (15.9), South Asia (13.2), and Western Africa (11.7). Another metric for understanding allelic diversity is to simply count the total number of unique alleles which are observed in each subcontinental group. Eastern African subcontinental groups have the highest number of total alleles observed across all HLA loci with a mean of 47.4 alleles per locus, which is supported by previous studies 33, 34, 35, 36 . This Eastern African allele diversity is highly concentrated to A, B, and C with 304, 261, and 347 total alleles respectively. Notably, this subcontinental group shows the highest number of alleles at HLA-DPB1 (199), a locus with a median of 34.0 alleles per group.

Estimating the effect of group size on MAD: In order to determine the effect that group size has on MAD, we ran a series of simulations based on the underlying data to see if trends remained after equalizing group sizes. We sampled with replacement all subcontinental groups down to 30 individuals per group and calculated allele frequency and MAD statistics for each group (Supplemental Figure S7). We repeated this simulation 1,000 times and empirically derived a 95% confidence interval based on the values observed in the simulations. While the exact numbers derived from the simulated MAD analysis did not match the values observed in the GAIA dataset, the conclusions derived from the simulations were the same: HLA-B was the most variable region based on MAD-50 and MAD-90 as well as AMRS, AMRN, and AFRE being the most variable subcontinental groups based on MAD-50 and MAD-90. One exception is made for the ratio of MAD-90:MAD-50 which does not show the same sort order as the observed ratio in the main text. This is likely due to the fact that MAD-90 values in a simulated small group derived from a diverse group are likely to be depressed due to a bottleneck artifact of the simulation. In a diverse group, much of the total frequency mass is spread across many rare alleles. Downsampling is more likely to miss rare alleles entirely and the few alleles that do survive the bottleneck are the ones that were already relatively common. In a less diverse group, most alleles are already at moderate frequency and survive the downsampling more or less intact and the shape of the frequency distribution is better preserved.

Bootstrapping to produce confidence intervals for allele frequencies and MAD:

To obtain confidence intervals for the allele frequencies we resampled alleles with replacement randomly from the pool of observed alleles within each subcontinental group, drawing alleles equal to the original group size. For each of 1,000 bootstrap replicates, the pool of alleles was established and then allele frequency was calculated from the simulated pool. We then derived 95% confidence intervals for both allele frequencies and MAD values using the percentile method, taking the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the resulting bootstrap distributions. Similarly, for MAD we established a pool of individuals equal to the group size and calculated MAD from that pool over 1,000 bootstrap replicates.

FCGR haplotype of origin: All haplotypes called for FCGR originate from the HPRC v2 graph referenced above which is primarily composed of 1kGP samples (plus HG002 and linear references). We conducted an analysis of the composition of the origin of each subcontinental group's haplotype coloring them based on the subcontinental group of the 1kGP sample from which the haplotype was first identified (Supplemental Figure S4) this is referred to as the graph-based haplotype of origin. This analysis revealed expected group trends in FCGR2 and FCGR3 where the majority of graph-based haplotypes of origin in each subcontinental group matched the subcontinental group but these trends were not observed in FCGR1. needed to reach the threshold. The values are calculated for both with and without 1kGP trios. Columns: Group code, Locus, 1kgp Trio Probands, MAD-X, Allele Count, Alleles.

Genotyping of IGHC:

We genotyped IGH constant regions across the genes IGHG1, IGHG2, IGHG3, IGHG4, and IGHGP using T1K and a custom database (described below) encompassing IMGT alleles and novel alleles detected in HPRC haplotype-resolved genome assemblies.

Custom IGHC Database: The database for IGHC was created using the IMGT published alleles which can be found here: https://www.imgt.org/IMGTrepertoire/index.php?section=LocusGenes&repertoire=genetable&sp ecies=human&group=IGHC in addition to the unique alleles which were present in the 232 HPRC Release 2 assemblies (https://humanpangenome.org/hprc-data-release-2/) and hs1 reference. The IGH genes in the assemblies were identified via liftoff 28 with the method outlined in the HPRC marker paper 25 with a sequence identity threshold of 90%. Coding sequences were compared to determine unique alleles and number of unique alleles for each locus are noted in Supplemental Table S21. Each coding sequence was padded with 200 base pairs of intronic sequence and joined with N's where intronic gaps were not spanned. The custom IGHC database is available on Zenodo: Supplemental Material S2.

Integration of Novel Allele Calls: T1K claims the ability to produce novel allele calls via single nucleotide variants relative to the alleles in the given database. The primary callset only integrates these novel calls when they result in an exact match to the coding sequence of any other IMGT allele and an absence of a match to the original predicted allele's coding sequence.

While this analysis allowed for calling of alleles which were added in a newer IMGT release (v3.63 vs v3.59), novel calls were also integrated if they resulted in a match to another allele which was already in the current database. The validation of this method can be found below in the section "Validation of Novel Allele Calls". A summary of incorporated, novel allele calls can be found here: Supplemental Table S22. All novel allele calls and their counts can be found in Supplemental Table S23.

Validation of Novel Allele Calls: Novel allele calls made by T1K were incorporated if they produced an exact match in the coding sequence of another IPD-IMGT/HLA published HLA allele. Our genotyping graph given to T1K relied on alleles from the v3.59 (2025-01) release and we validated any allele calls which were a match to the coding sequence released in the v3.63 Supplemental Tables Table S1. Figure 3. Majority allelic diversity (MAD) quantifies the allelic breadth required for group coverage. A-B) Number of alleles to ensure 50% (MAD-50, A) or 90% (MAD-90, B) of individuals in a group carry at least one allele from the set across HLA-A, -B, -C, and -DRB1 for each continental group. Subcontinental group assignment outside of continental supergroup:

There were two instances of assignment of subcontinental group outside of the direct continental subgroup affecting 216 individuals, the vast majority affecting samples in the 1kGP or HGDP. 116 African Caribbean in Barbados (ACB) and 74 African Ancestry in USA SW (ASW) assigned to the subcontinental North America group and continental Africa as well as 26 individuals in HGDP from the Mozabite population of Mzab, Algeria assigned to the Northern African group and continental Asia. In each of these assignments, we sought to preserve continental grouping as a method of ancestry evaluation and subcontinental grouping as a reflection of the modern day location of these individuals.

against the 2018 exome sequencing results at simulated depths of 5×,10×, and 30× for 330 samples from 1kGP. Recall and precision were calculated based on the sample-matched allele calls at each locus. False positives are alleles which are in our set, but not in the gold standard set. False negatives are alleles which are in the benchmarking set, but not in our set. True positives are alleles matched between both sets. Both HLA*LA and T1K performed well with F1-scores above 0.73 at HLA-A, -B, -C and DRB1. At 5× coverage, T1K consistently outperformed HLA*LA across HLA-A, B, and C with an F1-score of 0.80 compared to 0.76 for HLA*LA. Kourami displayed high recall (> 0.73) but due to a large number of ambiguous genotype calls suffered from low precision which drove the overall F1-score down. At 30×, T1K of HLA Loci: We genotyped classical HLA class I (A, B, C), class II (DPA1, DPB1, DQA1, DQB1, DRB1, DRB3, DRB4), non-classical HLA class I (E, F, G), and other MHC loci (MICA, MICB, TAP1, TAP2) using two different tools: T1K and HLA*LA.

Additional HLA loci were called with T1K only (DMA, DMB, DOA, DOB, DPA2, DPB2, DQA2, DQB2, DRA, DRB5, H, HFE, J, K, L, N, P, R, S, T, U, V, W, Y). These tools were run with default parameters. HLA*LA makes use of a pangenome graph with IMGT nomenclature which can be found here: http://www.well.ox.ac.uk/downloads/PRG_MHC_GRCh38_withIMGT.tar.gz and T1K took as an input IMGT coding sequences for each locus. Each coding sequence was padded with 200 base pairs of intronic sequence and joined with N's where intronic gaps were not spanned. T1K

Gamma Receptors:We genotyped genes in the Fc Gamma Receptor gene family using Locityper and a pre-release version of the HPRC v2.0 graph. FCGR1A, FCGR1BP, FCGR2A, FCGR2B, FCGR2C, FCGR3A, FCGR3B, and FCGBP were genotyped in GRCh38 coordinates using the following graph: https://s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/human-pangenomics/pangenomes/scratch/2025_02_28_ minigraph_cactus/hprc-v2.0-mc-grch38/hprc-v2.0-mc-grch38.raw.vcf.gz. Due to an exceedingly large variant spanning the FCGRT locus in the GRCh38-based graph, this gene was genotyped in the hs1-based graph using the following resource: s3://human-pangenomics/pangenomes/scratch/2025_02_28_minigraph_cactus/hprc-v2.0-mc-ch m13/hprc-v2.0-mc-chm13.raw.vcf.gz. Both graphs were then processed according to the best practices explained in: https://locityper.vercel.app/input_output. After graph processing, reference k-mer counting, and locus addition, raw reads were then pre-processed and genotyped with default parameters.

Figure S7.

FigureS7. Confidence intervals for MAD calculations derived from sampling with replacement to determine effect of group size. To determine the effect that group size has on MAD, we ran a series of simulations based on the underlying data to see if trends remained after equalizing group sizes. We sampled with replacement all subcontinental groups down to 30 individuals per group and calculated allele frequency and MAD statistics for each group. The middle 95 percentile of outcomes were used to calculate confidence intervals on the number of alleles to guarantee that 50% of individuals in a group have at least one allele in the set (MAD-50, A) or 90% of individuals (MAD-90, B) across HLA-A, -B, -C, and -DRB1 for each continental group. The same analysis was performed at the subcontinental group level for percentages between 50-90 (C), 50 (D) and 90 (E) in addition to F) the ratio of HLA-B MAD-90 to MAD-50 for each subcontinental group.
